title: Ten of Wands: See How Responsibilities and Burdens Are Distributed

quickTake.upright: Everything is weighing on you; it is time to redistribute the load
quickTake.reversed: To put a burden down, first arrange its handover and destination

hook: Ten long staffs gather in one person’s arms, bending the body forward. The Ten of Wands shows that individual tasks may each have value while the total load still needs to be calculated.

sections.title: Ten staffs gathered in one pair of arms
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Beneath a pale blue sky, a figure in a reddish-brown tunic and pale hose steps toward the right. The upper body leans markedly forward as both arms gather ten long staffs in front. They overlap close to the body and spread outward at their tops, where green leaves still grow. The figure’s head is lowered, with the face almost hidden by arms and wood.

Pale walls, red roofs, and trees appear in the lower-right distance. Space remains between figure and buildings, and no one else helps carry the staffs. The ground is level, not uphill. We can see concentrated weight and effortful forward movement, but cannot know the person’s expression, destination, or remaining travel time.

Leaves still grow at the tops of all ten staffs: a burden can consist of many valuable things. The problem is that they are crowded into one pair of arms, even obscuring the view ahead. A modern reading need not first label tasks “necessary” or “unnecessary.” Start with total quantity and carrying method. The distant buildings provide direction but no scale. “Nearly there” may be a wish or a fact; actual deadlines and remaining work must establish which.

sections.title: Success itself can become a burden
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Waite places burden and oppression at the card’s center, while also noting that gain or success can themselves create pressure. He acknowledges multiple old interpretations that are difficult to reconcile. “Too many good things may also become unbearable” is therefore a historical clue worth retaining.

This article develops that clue into a modern exercise on total responsibility and division of work. It reads reversal as a change in the existing way of carrying things, then examines how the change occurs. This is not an item-by-item translation of the old reversed terms concerning difficulties and complications.

sections.title: Understanding the upright card
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Upright, the card suits checking whether the workload matches available time, energy, and support. Pressure may come from too many tasks, unclear roles, excessive standards, or frequent switching. Identifying the specific bottleneck helps more than labeling yourself insufficiently capable.

Sort tasks into those requiring your responsibility, those open to shared responsibility, those that can shrink or wait, and those already finished but still occupying attention. If work genuinely needs to be concentrated temporarily, add an ending condition: until when, who must provide what support, and how will normal distribution resume afterward?

sections.title: Understanding the reversed card
sections.bodyMarkdown:
The reversal can prompt checking whether the load has actually changed. Shared responsibility, clear handovers, and reduced scope may make pressure manageable. Releasing some control so others can complete work as agreed may also be necessary.

If you merely stop looking, pass something to another person without explanation, or let every arrangement lapse at once, the tasks may remain. Verify actual changes rather than use a card to decide who is avoiding responsibility. Ask: “Where will this staff go after I release it?” A clear destination makes adjustment easier to sustain.

Upright in a strengths position, the card may describe your ability to connect complex tasks, while still requiring a check that this capacity is not being used without limit. Reversed in an outcome-after-adjustment position, it can ask whether burdens have genuinely decreased, rather than announce permanent ease. Evidence of a successful handover is that others can finish independently and the original person no longer owns all reminders and rework.

sections.title: Why is the same person still exhausted after chores are divided?
sections.bodyMarkdown:
**Original fictional case.** Yushan and her housemates each claim cleaning tasks, but she still notices what is missing, reminds everyone when to act, and checks who forgot. Everyone says they are willing to help, yet she reaches each weekend exhausted. Her question is: “We divided the chores, so why do I still feel responsible for everything?” She draws the Ten of Wands upright in the source-of-load position.

The figure gathers ten staffs together, resembling many individually small matters concentrated on one person. The facts show that dividing execution is not the same as dividing responsibility: noticing, deciding, and prompting also consume sustained attention. Upright can help name this invisible work without first judging the housemates selfish. The picture’s absence of help depicts one moment of concentrated load, not proof that no support can be negotiated in reality.

If housemates previously volunteered for whole tasks but she repeatedly took them back, the issue also involves allowing different methods. If they explicitly refuse any negotiation, the living arrangement needs reassessment; improving her checklist alone cannot solve it. Their actual responses determine what follows. The card does not predetermine blame.

She selects replenishing household supplies and proposes that one housemate fully own checking stock, buying, and recording, with only a budget and minimum stock level agreed. After two weeks, she will check whether she is giving fewer reminders, not merely whether the visible task division looks equal.

sections.title: Putting down responsibility means enabling the next person to receive it
sections.bodyMarkdown:
**Original fictional case.** Zhuowen wants to hand coordination of a hobby club’s events to a new volunteer. The volunteer is willing, but registration forms, venue contacts, and practical notes remain scattered through Zhuowen’s chat history. He fears events will stall if he leaves. His question is: “How can I step down after three years coordinating the club?” He draws the Ten of Wands reversed in the handover-advice position.

A modern reversal can move the ten staffs from tightly gathered to redistributed, but “letting go” alone is insufficient. A willing successor exists; the obstacle is that information and decision-making authority remain concentrated in the original coordinator. The obscured view also suggests a handover should let the successor see the full process, rather than return to Zhuowen with every problem.

Another possibility is that the new volunteer offered help for one event, not long-term coordination. Without clarifying scope, handing over everything would create a new burden. If the club has grown beyond any one volunteer’s capacity, roles should also be split instead of finding the next person to carry everything alone.

Zhuowen first confirms the scope, organizes essential contacts, procedures, and open tasks, and lets the new coordinator independently lead one planning session. He answers questions only at agreed times. After the event, he specifies his departure date and any unfinished handover items, giving reduced workload verifiable completion conditions.

sections.title: A small exercise
sections.bodyMarkdown: Give one staff in your arms the name of a real task. Ask: why am I carrying it, what would actually happen if it were not done this week, and how could it shrink or be handed over? Turn the adjustment into a discussable sentence, such as “I can finish A this week; if B must be finished too, the deadline needs to change.”

sections.title: Common misreadings
sections.bodyMarkdown: Distant buildings do not prove that “one more push will bring success,” and a lone carrier does not prove no one will help. Learning from the Ten of Wands means checking available support, requests already made, and reasonable divisions of work, rather than treating endurance as the outcome.

# Ten of Wands: See How Responsibilities and Burdens Are Distributed

Upright in one sentence: Everything is weighing on you; it is time to redistribute the load.

Reversed in one sentence: To put a burden down, first arrange its handover and destination.

Ten long staffs gather in one person’s arms, bending the body forward. The Ten of Wands shows that individual tasks may each have value while the total load still needs to be calculated.

## Ten staffs gathered in one pair of arms

Beneath a pale blue sky, a figure in a reddish-brown tunic and pale hose steps toward the right. The upper body leans markedly forward as both arms gather ten long staffs in front. A modern reading need not first label tasks “necessary” or “unnecessary.” Start with total quantity and carrying method. ## Success itself can become a burden

Waite places burden and oppression at the card’s center, while also noting that gain or success can themselves create pressure. He acknowledges multiple old interpretations that are difficult to reconcile. “Too many good things may also become unbearable” is therefore a historical clue worth retaining.

This article develops that clue into a modern exercise on total responsibility and division of work. It reads reversal as a change in the existing way of carrying things, then examines how the change occurs. This is not an item-by-item translation of the old reversed terms concerning difficulties and complications.

## Understanding the upright card

Upright, the card suits checking whether the workload matches available time, energy, and support. Pressure may come from too many tasks, unclear roles, excessive standards, or frequent switching. Identifying the specific bottleneck helps more than labeling yourself insufficiently capable.

Sort tasks into those requiring your responsibility, those open to shared responsibility, those that can shrink or wait, and those already finished but still occupying attention. If work genuinely needs to be concentrated temporarily, add an ending condition: until when, who must provide what support, and how will normal distribution resume afterward?

## Understanding the reversed card

The reversal can prompt checking whether the load has actually changed. Shared responsibility, clear handovers, and reduced scope may make pressure manageable. Releasing some control so others can complete work as agreed may also be necessary.

If you merely stop looking, pass something to another person without explanation, or let every arrangement lapse at once, the tasks may remain. Verify actual changes rather than use a card to decide who is avoiding responsibility. Ask: “Where will this staff go after I release it?” A clear destination makes adjustment easier to sustain.

Upright in a strengths position, the card may describe your ability to connect complex tasks, while still requiring a check that this capacity is not being used without limit. Reversed in an outcome-after-adjustment position, it can ask whether burdens have genuinely decreased, rather than announce permanent ease. Evidence of a successful handover is that others can finish independently and the original person no longer owns all reminders and rework.

## Why is the same person still exhausted after chores are divided?

**Original fictional case.** Yushan and her housemates each claim cleaning tasks, but she still notices what is missing, reminds everyone when to act, and checks who forgot. Everyone says they are willing to help, yet she reaches each weekend exhausted. The figure gathers ten staffs together, resembling many individually small matters concentrated on one person. The facts show that dividing execution is not the same as dividing responsibility: noticing, deciding, and prompting also consume sustained attention. Upright can help name this invisible work without first judging the housemates selfish. The picture’s absence of help depicts one moment of concentrated load, not proof that no support can be negotiated in reality.

If housemates previously volunteered for whole tasks but she repeatedly took them back, the issue also involves allowing different methods. If they explicitly refuse any negotiation, the living arrangement needs reassessment; improving her checklist alone cannot solve it. Their actual responses determine what follows. She selects replenishing household supplies and proposes that one housemate fully own checking stock, buying, and recording, with only a budget and minimum stock level agreed. After two weeks, she will check whether she is giving fewer reminders, not merely whether the visible task division looks equal.

## Putting down responsibility means enabling the next person to receive it

**Original fictional case.** Zhuowen wants to hand coordination of a hobby club’s events to a new volunteer. The volunteer is willing, but registration forms, venue contacts, and practical notes remain scattered through Zhuowen’s chat history. He fears events will stall if he leaves. His question is: “How can I step down after three years coordinating the club?” He draws the Ten of Wands reversed in the handover-advice position.

A willing successor exists; the obstacle is that information and decision-making authority remain concentrated in the original coordinator. ## A small exercise

Give one staff in your arms the name of a real task. Ask: why am I carrying it, what would actually happen if it were not done this week, and how could it shrink or be handed over? Distant buildings do not prove that “one more push will bring success,” and a lone carrier does not prove no one will help. Learning from the Ten of Wands means checking available support, requests already made, and reasonable divisions of work, rather than treating endurance as the outcome.
